facts.claim: "Jesse" is track 3 on Charles Wesley Godwin's second album How the Mighty Fall, released November 5, 2021.
"Jesse" was co-written by Charles Wesley Godwin and Zach McCord.
How the Mighty Fall was produced, mixed and engineered by Al Torrence and mastered by Garrett Haines.

Torrence also worked on Godwin's debut Seneca. Musicians on How the Mighty Fall include Eric James (acoustic guitar, backing vocals), Ben Townsend (fiddle, banjo), Joe Pinchotti (drums), Nate Catanzarite (bass) and Max Somerville (piano, Rhodes). The review does not break down who plays on "Jesse" specifically.
Godwin wrote "Jesse" after seeing spray-painted graffiti under a bridge on a run. He wondered who wrote the message and why, and began the song soon afterward.
In a 2021 interview Godwin said he has often seen things spray-painted on walls, trains and overpasses, and wonders about the circumstances behind them. He gave this as the story behind "Jesse".
Americana Highways describes "Jesse" as built on lovelorn graffiti under a bridge, from which Godwin paints a full story.

The album moves away from the autobiographical songs of Seneca toward character-driven songs about mortality, hope and regret. It was made during the pandemic touring halt, when Godwin's son was born and his family moved back to West Virginia.
Country Chord ranks "Jesse" among Godwin's top songs. It calls the song a messy breakup told by an unidentified third-party narrator.
Godwin was born May 18, 1993 in Morgantown, West Virginia. He began at West Virginia University in 2012 hoping to play football, was cut from the team, and turned to music.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Appalachian country-folk storytelling tradition of West Virginia, described by sources as traditional country informed by folk, with character-driven narratives.

draft:
Somebody spray-painted a question under a bridge in bright red letters: "Jesse do you miss me like I miss you tonight?" **Jesse** starts there, on a walk past that spot under the log-truck route, and Charles Wesley Godwin builds a whole broken love affair out of one line of graffiti. That's close to how it really happened. Godwin has said he saw the message while out on a run, wondered who wrote it and why, and started the song soon after. He has talked about how often he notices words painted on walls, trains and overpasses, and how he can't help imagining the circumstances behind them. He co-wrote this one with Zach McCord, and it's a clear example of the turn he took on How the Mighty Fall, away from the autobiographical songs of his debut Seneca and toward characters living with regret.

The narrator isn't the heartbroken one, and isn't Jesse. It's a passerby who has decided they know the whole story, and they aren't gentle about it. The chorus shuts like a door: "Jesse don't hear you and neither do I." The verses lay out the charges. The writer had the chance to confess and didn't, and they swore a love that would last until death. Then comes the sharpest line in the song, cutting at the gap between big words and small courage: "But only so much that you wrote it in red." That is love declared in paint, to a concrete wall, where Jesse will never read it. By the short middle section Jesse has someone else, with a ring on her hand, and the chance is gone.

But look at the frame. The song opens and closes on the same two lines, back under that bridge a week later, as if the narrator can't stop walking past it. Nobody spends a week scolding a stranger's graffiti unless it got to them. Contempt and fascination sit side by side, and the song never says which one is stronger. Maybe the coldness is just how the narrator keeps from feeling the same loss.

The music doesn't take sides either. A fingerpicked acoustic pattern moves at a slow, unhurried pace, and Godwin's voice is slightly raspy and mid-range, single-tracked with no harmony to soften the judgment. A second acoustic guitar strums underneath, a bass holds a simple line, and steel guitar slides in with long sustained notes. The arrangement fills out without getting louder, and the room sounds close. Al Torrence produced the album during the pandemic touring halt, when Godwin moved his family back to West Virginia. This is Appalachian country-folk storytelling, the old habit of singing someone else's trouble. Godwin bends it by making the teller a judge who can't quite walk away.

You come away wondering who you'd be in that story: the one who painted the words, or the one who couldn't stop reading them.
